post1.text:
Most companies that stall between $50M and $500M don't have a strategy problem. They have a leadership problem that looks like a strategy problem.

When organizations hire executives specifically to drive scale, as companies like Strive Health have done to expand their value-based care model, they are making a calculated bet: the right leadership architecture is the growth plan.

Here is what that means in practice for founders and CEOs at this stage:

1. The skills that got you to $50M are not the skills that get you to $200M. Leadership capacity has to be rebuilt, not recycled.

2. Accountability structures break before headcount does. If your leadership team cannot operate without you in the room, you are the bottleneck.

3. Scaling is not a revenue event. It is a decision-making event. Who decides what, and how fast, determines your ceiling.

Leaders who treat executive expansion as a tactical hire rather than a structural shift almost always pay for it later.

What is the leadership decision your company keeps avoiding that is quietly capping your growth?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Stanford Graduate School of Business makes a point that every scaling company needs to hear: executives who rush AI adoption across their organizations without first understanding the underlying infrastructure, data quality, and change management demands are setting themselves up for expensive failure.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly in companies moving through the $50M to $500M range. The technology is rarely the issue. The leadership readiness is.

Before you scale any major capability across your organization, AI or otherwise, your executive team needs alignment on what success actually looks like, who owns outcomes, and what breaks first when volume increases.

The companies that scale well are not the fastest adopters. They are the most deliberate ones.

Read the full Stanford piece here and ask yourself whether your leadership team is ready for what comes next: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMirwFBVV95cUxOYVhzWHYzT1VheXhTVGVNSHgtQlFMMHFPZHFoUmxYQTJ2SllrZG91d2trSW1UTHdBdmlhNVB6Q2FZeDVUSnRkWm1qaFRaN3ZDR2JvXzdtbkkwVF9rbXBwZ3QtWFp3ME92aXVESVRrY1RVUF9HWnp0ZUNJYktpN180aGx2OURxdm4wc0Z6UU1CeFdhVTFrLTloQ05wLWgwVThrNjZkZXBIMWNHcUkzc2tv

post3.text:
Companies expanding their executive teams to drive growth are making the right instinct. But instinct is not enough.

In Chapter 1 of Rock Your Business, titled Lead Like Lives Depend On It, co-author Katherine Slain draws a line that most leadership conversations avoid: at the $50M-plus stage, leadership is not about inspiration. It is about precision. The decisions you make about who leads, how they lead, and what they are accountable for will either compress your timeline to $500M or quietly extend it by years.

Katherine's insight in this chapter reframes the entire idea of executive leadership during scale. It is not about filling seats. It is about building a system of leadership that does not require you to be the answer to every hard question.

That distinction changes everything about how you hire, develop, and hold leaders accountable.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

Leadership during a scaling phase is not about vision or culture decks. It is about decision-making architecture, accountability clarity, and the discipline to build a team that grows faster than the problems it faces. Here is what that actually looks like.

post1.text:
Most business owners treat their exit like a finish line. It is actually a starting gun — and if you have not been running toward it for years, you are already behind.

A recent Entrepreneur piece made this painfully clear: founders obsess over growth metrics and almost never build toward a sellable asset. The result is a company that performs well but transfers poorly.

Here is what $50M+ leaders need to understand:

1. Your multiple is not determined at the negotiating table. It is determined by the decisions you made two to five years earlier — clean financials, documented processes, and reduced owner dependency.

2. Revenue is not value. EBITDA quality, customer concentration, and recurring revenue profiles are what acquirers actually price.

3. The best exits are boring from the outside. Predictable, systemized businesses command premium multiples because they reduce buyer risk.

You can grow a great company and still leave significant money on the table at exit.

So here is the question: Are you building a business, or are you building an asset someone else would pay top dollar to own?

post2.text:
A recent piece from J.P. Morgan Private Bank walks through the core business exit strategies available to owners — from strategic sales to private equity recapitalizations to family succession.

It is a solid overview. But here is what it does not address: for companies in the $50M to $500M range, choosing the right exit structure is only half the battle. The other half is arriving at that decision with a business that is actually positioned to command the valuation you expect.

At Autobahn, we see it constantly. Owners pick the right exit vehicle but spent the prior decade optimizing for cash flow, not for transferable value. Those are two very different things.

If you are scaling past $50M and have not stress-tested your exit readiness, start there.

post3.text:
Founders pour years into building revenue. Very few pour the same energy into maximizing what that revenue is actually worth to a buyer.

Chapter 2 of Rock Your Business — titled 'Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit' — tackles this directly. Chapter authors Paul Belair and George Hohman work with owners at the $50M to $500M scale and they know what separates a good business from a high-multiple transaction.

One thing they make clear early: the factors that drive your valuation multiple are not the same factors that drove your growth. Conflating the two is one of the most expensive mistakes a founder can make.

If exit is anywhere on your horizon — five years out or fifteen — this chapter will change how you think about every decision you make between now and then.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because of bad strategy, but because execution is treated as an afterthought.

Harvard Business School research confirms what we see constantly with scaling companies: the gap between planning and doing is where growth stalls. Leaders invest weeks building a beautiful plan, then hand it off and wonder why nothing changes six months later.

Here is what actually works at the $50M to $500M stage:

1. Strategy and execution cannot live in separate conversations. The people building the plan must own the outcomes.

2. Quarterly checkpoints beat annual reviews every time. Markets shift. Your cadence has to match that reality.

3. Accountability without visibility is just wishful thinking. If your team cannot see progress in real time, they are guessing.

Scaling companies do not fail because leaders lack vision. They fail because vision never connects to the daily work happening three levels down.

What is the single biggest breakdown point between strategy and execution inside your organization right now?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Harvard Business School Online broke down what separates managers who successfully implement strategy from those who watch it collect dust.

The findings align with everything we see working with companies scaling past $50 million: execution is not a soft skill, it is a system.

At Autobahn, we tell clients that a strategy document without an operating rhythm behind it is just expensive fiction. The companies that scale fastest are not the ones with the most sophisticated plans. They are the ones who build the habit of returning to the plan weekly, adjusting fast, and holding the right people accountable.

If your strategic plan is not driving decisions every single week, it is time to rethink how execution is structured inside your business.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiZ0FVX3lxTE5pcmMwWURjZ3NNYXZQOUI4V1Vwalk4TTJORHlsOEZOM2FlZG9ZSmw1LWFGc0RIYzNOcFNZbTkxRFhjWjdTdWkzek04UEhLblBJdWVUaGg2ZEsyeHJKd01YTXV6QXpTb2M

post3.text:
Strategy and execution look very different when your company is actually on the line.

In Chapter 3 of Rock Your Business, titled 'What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes,' authors Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall share what it really takes to move from having a plan to building a business that executes one consistently.

The chapter draws from real experience running businesses where the margin for misalignment was zero. One insight that stands out: the companies that scale do not have better strategies than their competitors. They have better systems for making sure the strategy shows up in every decision, at every level, every single week.

There is a specific approach Rafa and Jim outline that most $50M companies have never tried. We will let you discover it for yourself.

Rock Your Business, the new book from Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most companies above $50M don't have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit.

There's a difference. A habit is what your team does when no one is watching. A strategy is what drives repeatable, predictable revenue growth, regardless of who's in the seat.

Bain research on B2B growth leaders found that the companies consistently capturing new customers aren't just working harder. They've built a repeatable system for identifying, targeting, and converting the right buyers, and they run that system with discipline.

Here's what leaders at the $50M to $500M stage get wrong:

1. They confuse a high-performing sales team with a sales strategy. People aren't a plan.
2. They optimize for closing, not for pipeline architecture. Closing is a symptom of upstream decisions you made months ago.
3. They let the revenue number define success without asking why it happened or whether it can happen again.

If your top rep left tomorrow, would your revenue follow?

That's not a people question. That's a strategy question.

post2.text:
A recent piece from Bain on B2B growth masters caught our attention here at Autobahn Consultants.

The finding is straightforward but uncomfortable: the companies that reliably capture new customers aren't relying on talent or hustle. They've built a repeatable formula, and they execute it consistently.

For companies scaling from $50M and beyond, this is the gap that quietly kills momentum. Revenue grows, headcount grows, but the underlying sales motion never gets formalized. Leaders inherit what worked at $10M and wonder why it stops working at $100M.

The fix isn't a new CRM or a bigger quota. It's building a system that works without the heroics.

If your growth depends on a handful of people doing the right things at the right time, you don't have a sales strategy yet.

Read the Bain piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiuwFBVV95cUxNTnFuY29VYUwzZ2FBUUstT3NwOGJncXBFSm03ajFydXhEMUxzOVZRaXE0VndTOEtzX2ZfQUtySjJFX1F3ek1aTXRreFFJLUdyOWY1bWZ3RFZiTGNTNFlIVmtHVURtOW55bzBsVFREVXJudUE4TmhqZUVOSFZLUE5YNE1weU5NV0Rla3hxMW1oZDhTd3ZvR1lUQm9xRm04cFVQNUZBQ19lZnBxMnFBZXJjQVNNV2RWMWJsMmJV

post3.text:
Bain's latest research on B2B growth confirms something Deb and Brandon lay out bluntly in Chapter 4 of our upcoming book.

The chapter is called 'Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation.' That title is not a metaphor.

At the $50M to $500M stage, the absence of a defined sales strategy isn't neutral. It's costly. Every quarter you operate without one, you are funding your competitor's growth with revenue you should have kept.

What Deb and Brandon make clear is that most scaling companies don't lack sales effort. They lack sales architecture. There's a specific structure that separates companies that grow through chaos from those that grow through design, and Chapter 4 walks you through where to start building it.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling people get when they interact with your company, and most $50M+ businesses are getting that feeling completely wrong.

Campari's approach to brand longevity proves the point. Rather than chasing trends, they anchor iconic brands in cultural moments that already matter to their audience. The brand becomes part of the experience, not an interruption of it.

Here is what scaling companies miss:

1. Brand consistency is not sameness. It is the same core feeling delivered across every touchpoint, even as your audience evolves.

2. Culture moves faster than campaigns. If your marketing calendar is built around launches instead of relevance, you are already behind.

3. Smell is not a metaphor. The sensory experience of your brand, how it sounds, feels, and yes, smells, determines whether people remember you or forget you.

At $50M, you built a product. At $500M, you need to build a brand people choose before they shop.

What does your company actually feel like to a first-time customer?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive on Ulta's CMO caught our attention, and it should catch yours too.

Ulta is threading a needle that most scaling companies never figure out: building long-term brand equity while simultaneously driving performance across every channel. They are not treating brand and demand as separate budgets with separate goals. They are treating them as one unified motion.

For companies growing through the $50M to $500M range, this distinction is critical. Too many leaders fund paid channels because the attribution is clean and cut brand investment because it is harder to measure. That trade-off quietly erodes the competitive advantage you spent years building.

Strong brands lower your customer acquisition cost over time. Weak brands make every marketing dollar work harder than it should.

Read the full piece and ask yourself where your budget actually reflects your priorities: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPRlFnSEozTXJJdnl5aWFJQTFGR0tkcnhrUnUyOTNZNlIwcHZiLWFnbm0tQ0FWZEZCTWZvdUFQeEFvQkIwOHdpMmZBR3I5WmNjRmFYb0xJMGhQWmJHYUdWUVdyWndOWTYwR1ZQQ2E4V1dMV2NrT0hpRzNaU1VKdUdoZHMwSFB4SlhYTkZKZ2hDdEdsSkJ6TW91UTZTWlNGaGVmcUE

post3.text:
JBL stopped building marketing around campaigns. Instead, they started building it around culture, meeting audiences inside the moments that already matter to them rather than interrupting those moments with ads.

That shift is exactly what Chapter 5 of Rock Your Business addresses.

Titled 'What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?' and authored by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West, this chapter challenges scaling companies to think beyond visibility and into sensory brand identity. Most marketing at the $50M level is loud. The best marketing at the $500M level is felt.

Kayli and Yasmin lay out a framework for understanding whether your brand is actually landing the way you think it is, or whether it is producing a smell you never intended.

If your marketing feels like everyone else's in your category, this chapter is for you.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. For companies pushing past $50M, the instinct to scale headcount alongside revenue is one of the most expensive mistakes we see. SHRM's recent research on 2026 hiring trends confirms what we already tell our clients: precision beats volume every time.

Here is what that actually means in practice.

First, role clarity before recruitment. If your leadership team cannot define what success looks like in a role at 90 days, you are not ready to hire for it. Second, your talent pipeline should be a business asset, not an HR function. The companies scaling fastest treat recruiting as a revenue-generating activity, not overhead. Third, bad hires at the $50M to $500M stage are not just costly, they actively slow your trajectory. One wrong senior hire can set a division back 18 months.

Growth at this level is not about filling seats. It is about building a team that can operate at the level you are headed to, not the level you are at today.

What is the most expensive hiring mistake your company has made, and what did it actually cost you?

post2.text:
A recent piece in PCT Magazine covered WorkWave's appointment of Melinda Vedder as their new Chief Human Resources Officer. On the surface, it reads like a standard executive announcement. For scaling companies, it is a signal worth paying attention to.

When a growth-stage company elevates HR to the C-suite with a dedicated, experienced leader, it is not a formality. It is a strategic declaration. The businesses we work with that successfully navigate the $50M to $500M range almost always share one trait: they stopped treating people operations as administrative and started treating it as a competitive advantage.

If your HR function is still reporting three levels below the CEO, your talent strategy is probably three moves behind your growth ambitions.

Is your people leadership sitting at the table where your biggest business decisions get made? It should be.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better companies. They make slower ones.

Most leadership teams at the $50M+ level are not suffering from a lack of data. They are suffering from an addiction to it. Oracle NetSuite recently published a list of 30 financial metrics businesses should track. Thirty. If your team is reviewing 30 metrics in a leadership meeting, you are not leading, you are auditing.

Here is what high-growth companies actually do differently:

First, they pick fewer metrics with sharper definitions. A KPI without a clear owner and a clear threshold for action is just a number on a slide.

Second, they treat lagging indicators as historical context, not decision-making tools. Revenue last quarter tells you what happened. It does not tell you what to do next.

Third, they review metrics at the right altitude. Operational data belongs with operators. Executive teams need the three to five numbers that signal whether the business is healthy or not.

How many of your current KPIs actually change a decision when they move?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Business.com walked through 14 tools companies can use to track KPIs. Solid list. But here is the thing nobody says out loud: the tool is rarely the problem.

For companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, the real issue is almost never a lack of tracking capability. It is a lack of agreement on what matters and why. Teams invest in dashboards before they have alignment on which numbers should actually drive decisions. The result is beautifully designed data that no one acts on.

Before your next tool purchase, ask your leadership team to write down the five metrics that would change how they run the business if those numbers moved. If you get five different answers, you have a strategy problem, not a software problem.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMingFBVV95cUxQcWNPSTVTUDVYYURoVkZKa0ItNEtQbmJqWlNJTlIzUVZqclAxMHFaajNobC1JbGNkZGZVajN6MWJLT1pJcXktVG10VG8zUUljdU43NU5WR1cyNDB4QkxONlJkb3hJR2FfNzdGZHd1VWhPbTktdU1vdTEzamFWY2ZFVDNKUFIwRG91ZDdWU1UyN2twNFpLd1JjU3EzTUpjdw?oc=5

post3.text:
There is a chapter in our upcoming book that every leadership team running a $50M+ business needs to read before their next planning session.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business is titled "Death by KPIs." It was written by Héctor Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, and it goes after one of the most common and costly mistakes scaling companies make: confusing measurement activity with management clarity.

One insight that will stick with you: there is a meaningful difference between tracking a metric and owning one. Most organizations do a lot of the former and very little of the latter. That gap is where accountability quietly disappears.

The rest of the chapter gives leadership teams a practical way to close it.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most executives are using AI wrong, and the productivity numbers prove it.

A recent Fortune report found that 90% of executives say AI has not meaningfully moved the needle on productivity. At the same time, companies are still cutting headcount. That combination should alarm any leader running a scaling business.

Here is what we see working for companies in the $50M to $500M range:

First, AI does not replace strategy. It accelerates execution. Leaders who treat it as a magic answer are disappointed. Leaders who treat it as a force multiplier on decisions they already make well are winning.

Second, the bottleneck is rarely the tool. It is the workflow around the tool. Most teams adopt AI without redesigning the process it touches.

Third, a third monitor showing live AI outputs during your workday changes how your team operates faster than any training program will.

The companies pulling ahead are not using more AI. They are using it more deliberately.

What is the one workflow in your business where AI could double output if the process around it was actually rebuilt?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune landed a number that should stop every scaling CEO mid-scroll: 90% of executives say AI has not improved productivity, yet layoffs tied to AI adoption are still happening.

That is a dangerous combination. You are absorbing the disruption without capturing the upside.

At Autobahn, we work with companies moving from $50M toward $500M, and the pattern is consistent. Leaders who see AI gains are not the ones who adopted the most tools. They are the ones who rebuilt the workflows those tools sit inside.

If your AI investment is not showing up in your numbers, the problem is not the technology. It is the operating structure around it.

Read the full Fortune piece and then ask yourself whether your team is set up to actually capture what AI can deliver.

post1.text:
The leaders most likely to destroy their companies are the ones who never doubt themselves.

Imposter syndrome gets treated like a flaw to fix. It is not. At the $50M+ level, it is often a signal that a leader is operating at the edge of their actual experience, which is exactly where growth happens.

Forbes recently reported that imposter syndrome does not fade as leaders climb higher. It follows them. The difference between leaders who crumble under that weight and those who perform through it comes down to three things.

First, they separate feelings of inadequacy from evidence of incompetence. These are not the same thing. Second, they build teams that compensate for genuine gaps rather than hiding those gaps from everyone. Third, they stop performing certainty for their people and start modeling how to think through hard problems.

Leaders who scale companies do not conquer self-doubt. They learn to lead alongside it.

What would you do differently if you stopped treating doubt as a weakness?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Bona Magazine makes a compelling case that imposter syndrome, handled correctly, can actually sharpen executive presence rather than erode it.

That framing matters a lot if you are running a company between $50M and $500M.

At that stage, you are regularly making decisions in territory you have never navigated before. Self-doubt is not a bug in that environment. It is information. The leaders who scale successfully are the ones who learn to use that signal to ask better questions, hire sharper people, and stay honest about where the business actually stands.

The problem is that most leadership development programs teach people to project confidence first and build competence second. That order eventually catches up with you.

If your leadership team is struggling to close the gap between where they are and where the business needs them to be, this article is worth your time.

post1.text:
The hardest thing for a $50M+ business leader to schedule is their own life.

Most founders treat personal priorities as whatever survives after the business gets its share. That is a strategy for regret, not legacy.

A recent Entrepreneur piece made this painfully clear: founders obsess over growth plans, hiring plans, even exit plans, but almost none build a deliberate plan for what their life looks like on the other side. The business gets a roadmap. The person running it does not.

Here is what changes when you fix that:

1. You make better capital allocation decisions because you know what the money is actually for.
2. You stop optimizing for revenue and start optimizing for optionality.
3. The people around you, family, team, partners, get a more present and intentional leader.

Life planning is not a soft skill. At this level of growth, it is a strategic discipline.

What would you do differently in your business today if you had written down exactly what you want your life to look like in ten years?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur landed on something most growth-stage founders quietly know but rarely say out loud: nearly every founder plans for business growth, but almost none plan for what comes after it.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly with companies scaling from $50M to $500M. The business plan is airtight. The personal vision is blank.

That gap is not just a life problem. It creates real strategic dysfunction. Leaders without a personal destination make reactive decisions, hold on too long, or exit and feel completely lost.

If you are leading a scaling company, your life plan and your business plan need to be in the same conversation, not in separate rooms.

Read the full article here and then ask yourself: what is the business actually building toward, for you?

Founders are great at planning for their companies. They are rarely great at planning for themselves.

Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business, titled Coming Up for Air, tackles exactly this. Written by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain, this chapter challenges leaders at the $50M to $500M level to treat their personal life with the same rigor they bring to their business strategy.

One of the core ideas: coming up for air is not a reward you earn after the company hits its numbers. It is a practice you build into the work itself, before burnout or a forced exit makes the decision for you.

If you have ever said you will focus on your personal life once things slow down, this chapter was written for you.
